output.reason: The supplied evidence from the paper's Features section explicitly states that the feature set is divided into five subgroups: length-based, lexical, morphological, syntactic, and semantic features. Specific examples are provided for each: length-based (sentence length in tokens/characters, extra-long words, LIX); lexical (Kelly list CEFR-level incidence scores, difficult/unlisted tokens, lemmatizer misses, log frequencies); morphological (variation and incidence scores of lexical categories, inflectional features, TTR variants, nominal ratio, pronoun-to-preposition ratio, lexical density, relative structures); syntactic (dependency arc length/direction, relative clauses in clefts, pre/postmodifiers); and semantic (SALDO-based average senses per token and per noun). This fully supports an answer to the question.

claims.text: The paper divides its features into five subgroups: length-based, lexical, morphological, syntactic and semantic features.
The features were developed based on information from previous literature and a grammar book for Swedish L2 learners.
Length-based features include sentence length in number of tokens and characters, extra-long words (longer than thirteen characters), and the traditional Swedish readability formula LIX.

Lexical features use the Kelly list (CEFR level and frequencies per lemma), incidence scores per 1000 words, incidence of words at each CEFR level, tokens above the text/sentence CEFR level, tokens not in the Kelly list, lemmatizer failures, and average log frequencies.

Morphological features include variation and incidence scores of lexical categories, punctuations, particles, sub- and conjunctions, inflectional information such as neuter gender nouns and verb form ratios, bilogarithmic and square root TTR, nominal ratio, pronoun-to-preposition ratio, lexical density features, and relative structures.

Syntactic features are based on dependency arc length (depth) and direction, incidence of relative clauses in clefts, and incidence of pre- and postmodifiers such as adjectives and prepositional phrases.
Semantic features rely on SALDO, a Swedish lexical-semantic resource, using the average number of senses per token and the average number of noun senses per noun.

The introduction notes that linguistic features explored for readability incorporate information from part-of-speech taggers and dependency parsers, and that cognitively motivated features have been proposed (e.g., Coh-Metrix).
Using word-frequency features alone was almost as predictive as combining all features at the document level, but the full feature set gave 7% higher accuracy at the sentence level.
